title: Richard Ford: Born to a World at War

Richard Ford: Born to a World at War
To mark The Times’s 175th birthday, Times editors asked writers to reflect on — and imagine a little bit about — the newspaper’s front page on the day they were born. Look up your own birthday page here.
The first thing I notice about the front page of The New York Times’s Feb. 16, 1944, edition is how much more content there is than in, say, last Friday’s offering. Twelve stories appeared on the day I was born 82 years ago — only five were given more than a sentence or two a week ago. Was there more news fit to print back then?
Of course, I realize The Times has physically shrunk over the decades. Also, a world war was on in 1944, and multiple combat fronts needed coverage (unlike today when maybe there’s a war going on, but maybe not). The United States back then had legitimate allies, and these countries — to one extent or another — had our fates in their hands and required reportage. There were, as well, two well-identified enemies — more if you count Italy (and some would say France). Reporting on these upped the word count.
On my birthday, front-page space was also allotted to the rumored Finnish-Russian peace negotiations; to an apparent coup in Argentina that foreshadowed the rise of Juan Perón; to the Brits’ blockade of the Bay of Biscay; to our troops pounding the sanctified Benedictine Monte Cassino Abbey in Italy, which German soldiers were using to store artillery. And then there was what President Roosevelt and Gen. Eisenhower had to say about this mournful destruction (they concurred, but with heavy hearts).
Plus, the home front demanded notice. The civilian population was dropping, but New York City apartment occupancy was at its highest in more than 20 years, stumping the experts. The war may have been a factor there. Inside pages contained news of the Office of Price Administration combating price gouging on poultry parts, and there were encouraging stories about war bond sales and about denials of reported “color” restrictions against American soldiers in England. A world war creates a lot of news.
